title: We Put Our Trust in the Lord of Heaven
intro: Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani relates in the Book of Songs that Ali ibn al-Jahm sent this poem to his brother at the start of his imprisonment under the caliph al-Mutawakkil. The prisoner sets the guarded courts of kings beside a door he can still approach in prayer. He asks what wealth is worth to a man who cannot part with it and what a lifetime’s experience has taught him to prize. The recitation ends with loyalty. In the diwan he goes on to warn his brother about men who only yesterday called themselves his friends.

translation: We put our trust in the Lord of heaven
and submitted to the workings of his decree.
1.sharh: Writing to his brother, he begins with “we”. Trusting God and accepting the course events have taken are two acts the brothers can share even while one of them is in prison.

translation: We braced ourselves for the changes the nights bring,
our once unwilling souls at last consenting.
2.sharh: He speaks of his own soul as something he has had to train. The word for yielding comes only after the work of preparing himself for reversals of fortune.

translation: The courtyards of kings are screened off,
but at God’s door the forecourt is open to all.
3.sharh: He pictures the approach to a ruler from outside, where a petitioner might be stopped before even reaching the door. At God’s door anyone may stand in that same space.

translation: I look to him alone to lift my affliction,
and I have sought refuge only in prayer.
4.sharh: The open door of the previous line now has a practical meaning for the prisoner. He can ask for his suffering to be lifted without first securing an audience.

translation: Why should I not tell my anguish and my grief
to one who never turns a deaf ear to a call?
5.sharh: He borrows Jacob’s words for his grief at losing Joseph in the Qur'an. The prisoner who has just accepted God’s decree can still tell God how much it hurts.

translation: The days wound us and tend our wounds,
and run their course with happiness and misery.
6.sharh: Time has two roles in a single image. The days inflict a wound, then take the place of the person who dresses it. Both happiness and misery arrive in their course.

translation: No length of staying put can turn sustenance away,
nor can a long life bring it.
7.sharh: For a man confined to one place, it matters that a long stay need not keep his livelihood from him. By the same reasoning, merely living longer cannot produce it.

translation: Wealth does a miser no good
if his riches are kept out of reach.
8.sharh: The same word for wealth comes twice. First it measures what the man possesses, then what he keeps from being put to use. The next line names the use he fears to make of it.

translation: No fortune perishes through giving,
and no generous man comes to grief through generosity.
9.sharh: He answers the miser’s fear in two stages, first for the money and then for its owner. Giving is no cause of ruin to either, he insists.

translation: Just as asking humbles some,
it honours others through what they give.
10.sharh: A single request affects two people. It exposes the need of the person who asks and gives the one approached a chance to earn honour by answering.

translation: We have milked both halves of time’s udder. We have seen
hardship and ease each take their turn.
11.sharh: He draws on a saying about milking every part of an udder. To have done that to time is to have had all it has to give, in his case one turn of adversity and another of ease.

translation: I did not grieve for the worldly ease that left me,
and no one surpassed us in bearing loss well.
12.sharh: The singular “I” answers for his own loss of fortune. With “us” he lays claim to a shared strength, as though patience in loss were an excellence in which one could take the lead.

translation: We did not give up our modesty when hardship touched us,
though some hardships strip us of modesty.
13.sharh: He preserves the feeling that keeps a person from doing something beneath their dignity. Remembering what need can drive people to makes the claim more exacting.

translation: We have learned by experience, as did those before us,
and nothing is more precious than loyalty.
14.sharh: He sets his elders’ experience beside his own and gives both the same verdict. The full poem goes on to name the kind of betrayal that makes a friend who stays true so precious.

1.1.1.head: تَوَكَّلَ
1.1.1.meaning: To entrust one’s affairs to someone and rely on them.

1.2.2-3.head: أَسباب القَضاء
1.2.2-3.meaning: “The means of the decree.” The circumstances through which what God has ordained comes about.

2.1.1.head: وَطَّنَ
2.1.1.meaning: To prepare oneself for something and grow accustomed to bearing it.

2.1.3.head: غَير
2.1.3.meaning: Change, here the turns that fortune takes. Al-Waaedh sings ghayr, a word al-Lihyani records in this sense. The diwan and the Book of Songs have ghiyar, reversals of fortune. Mardam Bek also records ghadr, treachery.

2.2.2.head: سامَحَ
2.2.2.meaning: To yield or give way willingly.

3.1.1.head: فِناء
3.1.1.meaning: The open space in front of a house or palace.

3.1.3.head: مُحَجَّبَة
3.1.3.meaning: Screened off, with access controlled by the ruler’s attendants.

3.2.3-4.head: مَبذول الفِناء
3.2.3-4.meaning: “With its forecourt freely offered.” Anyone with a petition may approach.

4.1.4-5.head: كَشف الضُّرّ
4.1.4-5.meaning: “Lifting my affliction.” Taking away the harm or hardship that has befallen me.

4.2.2.head: فَزِعَ
4.2.2.meaning: To turn to someone or something for refuge or help.

5.1.4.head: بَثّ
5.1.4.meaning: Grief so pressing that one gives it voice. The phrase recalls Jacob’s words in the Qur'an, 12:86.

5.2.4.head: صَمَّ
5.2.4.meaning: To be deaf to a call or turn a deaf ear.

6.1.3.head: كَلَمَ
6.1.3.meaning: To wound, to cut into the flesh.

6.1.4.head: أَسا
6.1.4.meaning: To tend or dress a wound.

7.1.4.head: رَدَّ
7.1.4.meaning: To turn back, here to keep someone’s sustenance from reaching them.

8.1.2.head: أَجدى
8.1.2.meaning: To be of use or benefit.

8.2.4-5.head: مَحظور الثَّراء
8.2.4-5.meaning: “With wealth kept out of reach.” The miser withholds his money from use.

9.1.5.head: نَوال
9.1.5.meaning: A gift, or the act of giving freely.

9.2.2.head: أُتِيَ
9.2.2.meaning: To be undone or suffer harm from a particular quarter.

11.1.1-3.head: حَلَبَ الدَّهرَ أَشطُرَهُ
11.1.1-3.meaning: “We milked both halves of time’s udder.” A she-camel has four teats, two to each half. The saying means to know life in both good times and bad.

11.2.2.head: عُقبَة
11.2.2.meaning: A turn or spell. The plural marks successive periods of hardship and ease.

12.1.2.head: أَسِفَ
12.1.2.meaning: To grieve for a loss. Mardam Bek prints the singular heard here and suggests the plural in a footnote.

12.2.5.head: العَزاء
12.2.5.meaning: Patience or composure in the face of loss.

13.1.2.head: وَدَعَ
13.1.2.meaning: To leave something behind or relinquish it.

13.1.4-5.head: مَسّ ضُرّ
13.1.4-5.meaning: “At the touch of hardship.” When distress overtakes someone.

14.1.3.head: الأَوَّلون
14.1.3.meaning: Those who came before us, our forebears.

14.2.3.head: أَعَزّ
14.2.3.meaning: More precious, with a suggestion of being hard to come by.
